images.title: The gap decides the HCF
images.purpose: Show that a common factor of two numbers must divide the gap between them, using 8 and 10, 9 and 11, and 12 and 13.
images.composition: One horizontal number line across the middle of the frame with three short arcs, two above and one below, and wide white margins.
exact_structure: One grey #6B7280 horizontal number line with exactly 6 equally spaced ticks, labelled 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 from left to right.
Arc 1, teal #0072B2, drawn above the line from 8 to 10, with the label HCF 2 above its top.
Arc 2, amber #E69F00, drawn below the line from 9 to 11, with the label HCF 1 below its bottom.
Arc 3, reddish purple #CC79A7, drawn above the line from 12 to 13, with the label HCF 1 above its top.
Each arc has a dot at both ends in its own colour: exactly 6 dots in total, on 8, 10, 9, 11, 12 and 13.
One caption line centred under the whole picture: A common factor must divide the gap.
labels: A common factor must divide the gap.
rejection: the teal arc not joining 8 and 10, the amber arc not joining 9 and 11, or the purple arc not joining 12 and 13
the pair 8 and 10 labelled with anything other than HCF 2
the pairs 9 and 11 or 12 and 13 labelled with anything other than HCF 1
more or fewer than 6 ticks or 3 arcs
images.takeaway: Two consecutive numbers have HCF 1, and two consecutive even numbers have HCF 2, because a common factor divides their gap.
images.description: A number line from 8 to 13 with arcs joining 8 and 10 (HCF 2), 9 and 11 (HCF 1) and 12 and 13 (HCF 1).
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on general statements about consecutive, even and co-prime pairs.
images.teaching_notes: Ask students how far apart the two ends of each arc are, then check which numbers can divide both ends.

image_decisions.why: A number line makes the gap between the pair, and so the possible common factors, visible at a glance.
